title: Non-blocking follow-ups from backend-position-watchlist-race-condition's PR #382 review
description: Tracked, non-blocking findings from pr-reviewer's review of PR #382 (backend-position-watchlist-race-condition, the concurrent-insert race fix for POST /api/portfolio/positions and POST /api/watchlist), including findings surfaced by a code-review skill pass. See that PR's review comment and docs/tasks/backend-position-watchlist-race-condition.json's review.comments for full context. None of these block the PR -- the race-handling it actually delivers (the brand-new-ticker insert race, exactly what the task's own checklist scoped) was verified correct via mutation testing (removing the try/except on each endpoint's insert path and confirming the new regression test for that endpoint then fails with an uncaught IntegrityError/OperationalError, then restoring it) and the full test/coverage/static-analysis/e2e suite passed. Every item below was independently confirmed, via `git show main:backend/app/api/routers/portfolio.py`, to be a pre-existing gap that predates this PR (not a regression it introduces) -- the original code already had a single unprotected `db.commit()` shared by both the insert and merge branches.

checklist.step: docs/architecture/API.md's 'Error Cases to Cover in Tests' list (and the per-endpoint sections for `POST /api/portfolio/positions`/`POST /api/watchlist`) wasn't updated to document the new 503 this PR added to both endpoints (a concurrent-insert conflict whose re-query finds no same-key winner row). Every other 503 addition in this codebase's history (e.g. the IBKR account-positions fetch, `GET /api/cftc/cot`, the day-trader-mode 503s) has a corresponding bullet in that list -- this PR's two new 503s are the one gap. `backend/openapi.json`/`frontend/src/api/types.ts` are correctly regenerated and up to date; only the architecture doc's own error catalog is stale.

Higher priority than the rest of this list -- a genuine silent-data-loss risk, not just an unhandled-500-then-retry nuisance: two concurrent `POST /api/portfolio/positions` requests for the SAME already-existing ticker is a classic lost-update race that this PR does not address (and wasn't scoped to -- the task's checklist specifically named 'the newly-constructed-row path'). Both requests load the same pre-commit `existing.quantity`/`avg_cost_basis` via `db.query(PositionORM).filter(...).one_or_none()`, each independently computes its own merged result from that same stale baseline in `_merge_position`, and the second `db.commit()` silently overwrites the first's already-committed merge with no exception raised at all (no unique-constraint violation triggers here, since this is an UPDATE to an existing row, not an INSERT) -- one of the two real position updates the user submitted vanishes with no error surfaced to either caller. This directly contradicts the principle this very PR's own `decisions` entry establishes for the insert-race case ('this request's payload is user-submitted trade data... must not be silently dropped'). Confirmed via `git show main:...` that this lost-update exposure already existed identically before this PR (the original code had one shared, equally-unprotected `db.commit()` for both the insert and merge branches) -- not a regression, but a more severe pre-existing gap than this followups task's other items, since the others only risk an unhandled 500 rather than silent corruption. Closing it properly likely needs a different technique than a try/except (e.g. an optimistic-concurrency version column with a conditional UPDATE, or SQLite `BEGIN IMMEDIATE`-style write locking around the read-modify-write), not just catching an exception -- a bigger design decision than this task's narrow insert-race scope, worth its own dedicated investigation.

Relatedly and more narrowly: neither the pre-existing already-exists-at-first-query merge path's `db.commit()` (backend/app/api/routers/portfolio.py, the `else` branch) nor the race-recovery merge's own second `db.commit()` (inside the new `except (IntegrityError, OperationalError)` block, after `_merge_position`) is wrapped in the same try/except this PR adds for the initial insert. A plain OperationalError from SQLite whole-file lock contention (no actual lost-update, just two unrelated concurrent writers) hitting either of these commits still crashes as an unhandled 500 instead of the graceful 503 this PR establishes as the endpoint's own convention for exactly this failure mode -- an inconsistency between the insert path (now hardened) and the two merge paths (still as fragile as before this PR). The race-recovery commit specifically is new code introduced by this PR, so this asymmetry is newly visible even though the underlying gap (an unprotected merge-commit) predates it.

The re-query for the concurrent winner (`db.query(PositionORM).filter(...).one_or_none()` in portfolio.py / `db.get(...)` in watchlist.py), run inside the `except (IntegrityError, OperationalError)` block, has no exception handling of its own -- a second OperationalError from continued SQLite lock contention at that exact moment (the re-query SELECT racing the same contention that caused the first exception) would propagate unhandled as a raw 500 rather than the intended 503. Narrow and timing-dependent; likely acceptable as an inherent limit of a single-level retry for a single-user MVP, but worth an explicit decision either way rather than leaving it implicit.

Reuse/simplification: the merge-then-commit sequence (`_merge_position(...); db.commit()`) is now duplicated at two call sites in portfolio.py (the race-recovery branch and the already-exists branch) with inconsistent error handling between them (per the item above), and the two endpoints' `except (IntegrityError, OperationalError)` blocks duplicate the same rollback -> re-query-winner -> (log+raise 503 if no winner) shape, differing only in the query form and what happens with a found winner (merge-and-commit vs just-return). If the lost-update/unprotected-merge-commit items above are ever addressed, consider extracting a single `_commit_merge(db, target_row, position, provider, ticker)`-style helper (or a shared rollback/re-query/503-or-found-winner skeleton) that performs the merge, commits, and catches the same way the insert path does, fixing the gap and removing the duplication in one place rather than two.

decisions.decision: Fixed the same-ticker merge lost-update race (checklist item 2, the highest-priority item) with SQLAlchemy's built-in optimistic-concurrency mechanism: a new `PositionORM.version` integer column (`default=1`, `server_default="1"`, migration 051c44cc730b_add_version_to_positions.py) wired up via `__mapper_args__ = {"version_id_col": version}`. Every UPDATE SQLAlchemy issues against a `PositionORM` row now carries `WHERE ... AND version = <value just read>` and an incremented `version` in its SET list; if that UPDATE affects 0 rows (because another transaction already committed a change to the same row since this session read it), SQLAlchemy itself raises `sqlalchemy.orm.exc.StaleDataError` -- exactly the detection the lost-update race was missing (a plain UPDATE to an existing row has no unique constraint to trip the way an INSERT does, so nothing previously raised at all). A new helper, `app.api.routers.portfolio._merge_and_commit`, wraps the merge+commit at both of `add_position`'s same-ticker call sites (the genuine already-exists branch, and the race-recovery merge after a losing insert) in a bounded retry loop (`_MAX_POSITION_MERGE_ATTEMPTS = 5`): on `StaleDataError` (or the pre-existing `IntegrityError`/`OperationalError` categories), it rolls back, re-queries the ticker's now-current row, and retries the merge against that fresh baseline -- the losing request's own user-submitted quantity/cost-basis is re-applied on top of the winner's already-committed data, never discarded, mirroring the exact principle this task's parent PR (#382) already established for the insert-race case.
decisions.rationale: Two alternatives from the checklist's own suggestion were seriously considered and rejected. (1) A hand-written conditional UPDATE (`UPDATE positions SET ... WHERE ticker = ? AND version = ?`, checking `rowcount == 1`) would give the identical correctness guarantee but requires reimplementing, by hand, exactly what SQLAlchemy's `version_id_col` already does for every ORM-issued UPDATE against this table -- more custom code with more surface for a subtle mistake (e.g. a future column added to `PositionORM` whose write path forgets to bump `version`, or a raw-SQL UPDATE that bypasses the check entirely), for no behavioral benefit over the built-in mechanism. (2) SQLite `BEGIN IMMEDIATE`-style pessimistic write locking around the whole read-modify-write was rejected for three reasons: (a) this app's engine/session setup (`app/db/session.py`) has no existing hook for per-transaction isolation-mode control, and `BEGIN IMMEDIATE` only for this one endpoint while every other write path keeps SQLite's default deferred transactions would be an inconsistent, partial application of pessimistic locking rather than a coherent app-wide policy; (b) SQLite's write lock is file-level, not row-level, so `BEGIN IMMEDIATE` would serialize ALL concurrent writes anywhere in the database for the whole duration of the read-modify-write, not just concurrent writes to the SAME ticker -- a strictly worse concurrency profile than optimistic locking for the common case of a growing portfolio with many different tickers; (c) for a single-user MVP where same-ticker contention is rare and transient (an accidental double-click, or a client retrying a request it believes timed out), paying a correctness-check cost only when a conflict actually occurs (optimistic) is preferable to paying a lock-acquisition cost on every single `add_position` call regardless of whether a conflict will ever happen (pessimistic). The retry bound of 5 was chosen as generous enough to absorb a realistic burst of same-ticker contention for this app's one plausible writer (the user themselves), while still bounded so a pathological, endlessly-contended merge surfaces as a clean 503 rather than retrying forever.

decisions.decision: Verified the lost-update fix with a genuine concurrent-update reproduction, not just a unit test asserting the code path exists, at two levels: (1) backend/tests/integration/test_portfolio_positions.py's `TestAddPositionMergeLostUpdateRace` uses a second, independently-committing real SQLAlchemy session (not a mocked exception) racing `db_session`'s own merge, so the `StaleDataError` it observes is the real one SQLAlchemy raises from a real 0-row-affected UPDATE; (2) backend/tests/integration/test_portfolio_positions_lost_update_race.py's `TestConcurrentMergeRaceRealHTTPConcurrency` goes further still -- two real OS threads, each with its own SQLAlchemy session bound to its own connection against a shared temp-file SQLite database (not the in-memory `StaticPool`-backed `db_session` fixture most of this suite uses, which shares one underlying connection and so can't model two genuinely independent writers), issuing two real concurrent HTTP requests through `TestClient`, synchronized with a `threading.Barrier` so both requests have genuinely both read the same pre-commit row before either is allowed to proceed to merge+commit. Both tests assert the final row reflects BOTH concurrent requests' own quantities (e.g. 10 original + 5 + 7 = 22), not just one of them. As the actual mutation test: `PositionORM.__mapper_args__`'s `version_id_col` line was manually commented out during development and all three of this task's new lost-update tests (the two above plus the direct minimal-reproduction test) were re-run and confirmed to FAIL in that state (the real bug reproduces: the second committer's merge silently overwrites the first, landing at 15.0 instead of 22.0, with `StaleDataError` never raised) before the line was restored and the suite re-confirmed green -- the tests genuinely catch the regression they're named for, not just exercise the code path.
decisions.rationale: The task's own instructions explicitly called for 'real mutation-testing of the fix with a real concurrent-update reproduction, not just a unit test asserting the code path exists', given this area's 'parallel DB usage without locks' theme. A purely mocked test (patch `commit` to raise `StaleDataError` directly) would prove the exception-handling code path runs, but would not prove the underlying SQLAlchemy mechanism (`version_id_col`) actually detects a real concurrent write the way this fix claims -- only a second, truly independent session committing a real conflicting change, and a real multi-threaded, multi-connection HTTP-level scenario, can demonstrate that. The temp-file-backed SQLite engine (not `:memory:`/`StaticPool`) was specifically chosen for the HTTP-level test because the existing `db_session` fixture's `StaticPool` shares one underlying DBAPI connection across all sessions bound to it, which cannot model two genuinely independent, concurrently-open transactions the way two real request-scoped sessions in production would.

decisions.decision: Checklist item 4 (the re-query for the concurrent winner having no exception handling of its own): decided to harden further rather than accept it as an inherent single-level-retry limit. `_merge_and_commit`'s re-query is now covered by the same bounded retry loop as the merge-commit itself -- if the re-query raises `OperationalError`, the loop simply retries the whole merge attempt from its last-known row rather than propagating the exception unhandled or giving up immediately. A genuinely empty re-query result (the ticker's row not found at all, e.g. a concurrent `DELETE /api/portfolio/positions/{id}`) is treated differently and still exits immediately with a 503 rather than retrying further -- a missing row is not a transient condition the next attempt is likely to resolve the way lock contention is, so retrying that case would just burn through `_MAX_POSITION_MERGE_ATTEMPTS` attempts for no benefit.
decisions.rationale: Once a bounded retry loop already existed for the StaleDataError/IntegrityError/OperationalError triad (needed for item 2 regardless), folding the re-query's own OperationalError into that same loop was a small, low-risk addition with a clear correctness benefit (closing a real gap the checklist flagged) rather than a separate, more complex mechanism -- there was no meaningful cost to choosing the more robust option here. The 'no row found' case was deliberately kept as an immediate exit (not retried) because retrying it provides no real recovery value: unlike lock contention (which resolves itself as the other writer's transaction completes), a position that's been deleted stays deleted for the rest of this request's lifetime, so retrying would only delay an inevitable 503 while consuming retry budget that a genuine lock-contention case might have needed.

decisions.decision: Checklist item 5 (reuse/simplification): extracted the shared `_merge_and_commit(db, existing, position, provider, ticker)` helper and used it at both of `add_position`'s merge-then-commit call sites (the already-exists branch and the race-recovery branch), replacing the previously-duplicated `_merge_position(...); db.commit()` pairs and their inconsistent error handling with one shared implementation.
decisions.rationale: This was a clean win rather than a forced refactor: fixing item 2 already required building one retry-capable merge-commit implementation, and both call sites needed exactly that same behavior (same failure modes, same recovery shape, same 503 convention) -- there was no reason for two independent copies once the correct behavior was defined once. The checklist's own suggested shape (a single `_commit_merge`-style helper) was followed directly; the two call sites' prior difference (`winner`/`existing` as the starting row, otherwise identical) collapses to a single parameter, so no behavioral compromise was needed to unify them.

decisions.decision: Fixed pr-reviewer's blocking PR #385 finding (`PositionORM.version`'s `version_id_col` silently extending SQLAlchemy's optimistic-concurrency check to DELETE statements, not only UPDATE, so `delete_position`'s own `db.delete(row); db.commit()` could raise an unhandled `StaleDataError` -> raw 500 if a concurrent merge/update bumped the row's version in the window between the DELETE's read and its commit) by choosing **retry-and-redelete**, not an immediate 503, as the DELETE-specific handling. New helper `_delete_position_and_commit` (backend/app/api/routers/portfolio.py) wraps `delete_position`'s delete+closed_trades-insert+commit in the same bounded retry shape `_merge_and_commit` already uses for the merge paths (`_MAX_POSITION_DELETE_ATTEMPTS = 5`): on `StaleDataError`/`IntegrityError`/`OperationalError`, it rolls back, re-queries the row via `db.get`, and -- since a delete has no 'combine both requests' data' concept the way a merge does -- resolves to exactly one of three outcomes: (a) the row still exists (the conflict was a concurrent UPDATE, not a DELETE) -> retry the whole delete, recomputing the `closed_trades` row's quantity/avg_cost_basis/entry_notes/strategy from that freshest committed state rather than the stale pre-race snapshot, so the realized P&L recorded reflects the position as it actually stood just before deletion; (b) the row is already gone (a concurrent DELETE beat this one to it) -> a `404`, since this request's own intended outcome (the position no longer existing) already happened -- treated identically to the ordinary not-found case at the top of `delete_position`, not a retry, since a deleted-elsewhere row isn't a transient condition another attempt could resolve differently; (c) genuine lock contention (including from the re-query itself) exhausts `_MAX_POSITION_DELETE_ATTEMPTS` -> the same 503 transient-conflict convention `_merge_and_commit` already establishes. `exit_price`/`exit_date` (the resolved values, whether from the live `latest_close()` lookup or a manual override) are computed once before the retry loop and reused across every attempt, since they reflect market timing/a caller-supplied override, not the row's own version state, and re-fetching market data on every retry would be both wasteful and pointless.
decisions.rationale: An immediate 503-on-any-conflict (the task's other suggested option) was rejected: for the dominant real case -- a concurrent merge bumped this row's version, but the row itself is completely intact and still needs deleting -- failing the request and making the caller retry from scratch provides no benefit over this app just doing that retry itself, exactly as `_merge_and_commit` already does for the analogous merge-commit conflict; forcing every DELETE to fail and be manually retried whenever it merely raced an unrelated UPDATE would be a strictly worse user experience for no correctness gain. The one genuine behavioral choice specific to DELETE (as the task framing itself flagged: there's no 'merge both requests' data' option here) was what to do when the re-query finds the row gone entirely -- 404 was chosen over folding that into the same 503-after-retries path because it's a *correctness* distinction, not just a transient-vs-exhausted one: a row that's merely contended (version bumped by an UPDATE) really is a transient condition a retry can resolve, but a row that's been deleted by someone else stays deleted for the rest of this request's lifetime, so retrying it would only consume retry budget for an inevitable outcome -- and 404 is also the exact status this same endpoint already returns for 'this position doesn't exist' one line above, so reusing it here is consistent rather than introducing a second, redundant not-found shape. Verified end-to-end via a real, genuinely-concurrent reproduction (`backend/tests/integration/test_portfolio_positions_lost_update_race.py`'s `TestConcurrentUpdateRacingDeleteRealHTTPConcurrency`: two real OS threads/connections, a real concurrent `POST /api/portfolio/positions` merge forced to complete during the live `latest_close()` fetch window `DELETE` takes by default, exactly the window pr-reviewer's finding described) plus targeted edge-case tests for the re-query-itself-failing, row-gone-on-requery, and retries-exhausted branches (`backend/tests/integration/test_portfolio_delete_position.py`'s `TestDeletePositionCommitRaceHandling`, mirroring `TestAddPositionMergeCommitRaceHandling`/`TestAddPositionMergeRetryBoundsAndRequeryHardening`'s existing pattern for the merge paths) -- real multi-thread concurrency for the primary scenario, controlled mocking only for the narrower branches real concurrency can't practically force. Mutation-tested per the review's own instruction: temporarily reverted `_delete_position_and_commit`'s `except` clause to drop `StaleDataError` (restoring the old unhandled behavior) and confirmed `TestConcurrentUpdateRacingDeleteRealHTTPConcurrency` failed with exactly the unhandled `StaleDataError` the finding described, then restored the fix and reconfirmed the full suite green. Also discovered and fixed, while regenerating the OpenAPI snapshot for this fix's own new 503 response: `frontend/src/api/types.ts` had already silently drifted out of sync with `backend/openapi.json` since this same PR's own prior commit (3085233b) changed `add_position`'s 503 description text without re-running `generate:api-types` -- this fix's regeneration (`npm run generate:api-types` from `frontend/`) catches up both that pre-existing drift and this fix's own new `delete_position` 503 response type in one pass; `npx tsc --noEmit` and the full frontend test suite (1031 tests) both pass against the regenerated types.

decisions.decision: Fixed pr-reviewer's round-2 blocking PR #385 finding (an uncaught `sqlalchemy.orm.exc.ObjectDeletedError` escaping as a raw 500 in both `_merge_and_commit` and `_delete_position_and_commit`, when the re-query inside their retry loops' `except` block itself fails with `OperationalError` -- leaving `row` un-refreshed and expired -- and the row then turns out to have been genuinely deleted by a different concurrent transaction before the next attempt touches it) by adding `ObjectDeletedError` to both functions' caught exception tuples, in both cases routing the attempt through the exact same rollback -> re-query -> row-gone handling each function already has for an ordinary concurrent-delete case: `_merge_and_commit` ends up at its existing `no_row_found_on_requery` 503 path (there's no row left to merge against, logically identical to a concurrent-delete-during-merge), and `_delete_position_and_commit` ends up at its existing `refreshed is None` 404 path (the row being gone IS this request's own intended outcome). `_delete_position_and_commit` additionally needed its per-attempt body (the `ClosedTradeORM` construction reading `row.ticker`/`row.quantity`/etc., plus `db.delete(row)`) moved inside the `try` -- it was previously built *before* the try/except even started, so the attribute access that actually triggers `ObjectDeletedError` wouldn't have been caught no matter what was in the except tuple.
decisions.rationale: Catching `ObjectDeletedError` directly (rather than, say, proactively re-querying the row a second time right after the inner re-query's own `OperationalError`) was preferred because it required no new control flow -- the existing exception-driven retry loop in each function was already built to roll back, re-query, and branch on whether a row was found; `ObjectDeletedError` is just one more way an attempt can discover 'this row is actually gone,' discovered one attempt later than usual (on the *next* iteration's attribute access, rather than at the original re-query), and routing it through the loop's existing re-query gives the correct, already-handled 404/503 outcome for free. A proactive extra re-query immediately after the inner `OperationalError` was considered and rejected: it would duplicate the exact re-query logic the loop already performs at the top of its next iteration (via `_merge_position`'s/the `ClosedTradeORM` construction's attribute access triggering the lazy reload), for no behavioral difference -- the outcome is identical either way, just reached one statement sooner, and the duplication would be a second place for exactly this class of bug to recur. Verified by writing a genuine regression test for each function (`TestAddPositionMergeRetryBoundsAndRequeryHardening.test_requery_operational_error_then_row_genuinely_deleted_raises_handled_503` in test_portfolio_positions.py; `TestDeletePositionCommitRaceHandling.test_delete_requery_operational_error_then_row_genuinely_deleted_raises_handled_404` in test_portfolio_delete_position.py), each using the same mocked-exception-injection pattern as this PR's existing edge-case tests (monkeypatching `commit`/`query`/`get`), with the re-query's own failure path additionally performing a real delete+commit of the row (mirroring the existing `test_merge_commit_conflict_with_no_row_found_on_requery_returns_503`/`test_delete_commit_conflict_with_row_gone_on_requery_returns_404` tests' technique) so the subsequent attribute access raises a genuine `ObjectDeletedError`, not a mocked one. Mutation-tested both: temporarily removed `ObjectDeletedError` from each function's except tuple, re-ran its new test, and confirmed it failed with the exact raw, unhandled `ObjectDeletedError` traceback the finding described (captured via pytest's own failure output, not just an assertion failure) -- then restored both fixes and reconfirmed the full backend suite green (1613 passed, 100% line/branch coverage) plus ruff/mypy clean and `openapi.json` byte-for-byte unchanged (no API-contract-visible change, this is purely internal error-handling hardening).

decisions.decision: Decided NOT to extract the shared retry-loop helper (already tracked as its own non-blocking item on docs/tasks/backend-position-watchlist-race-condition-followups-followups.json) as part of this fix, despite pr-reviewer's round-2 comment suggesting it be strongly considered now that this is the second related gap found in the same duplicated shape. Applied the identical narrow fix (add `ObjectDeletedError` to the except tuple, plus -- for the delete path only -- widen the `try` to cover the per-attempt body) to both `_merge_and_commit` and `_delete_position_and_commit` separately instead.
decisions.rationale: This PR is already on its third review round for what was originally scoped as a narrow same-ticker-merge lost-update fix; a structural extraction (designing a shared helper parameterized over merge-vs-delete's differing per-attempt operation, differing row-gone outcome (503 vs 404), and differing log-message wording) is itself a real design decision with its own surface for a new mistake, and bundling it into an already-multi-round blocking-fix pass raises the risk of yet a *third* subtle gap being introduced under the same time pressure that produced the first two -- exactly the failure mode this task's own fix is trying to close out, not add another instance of. The two fixes, applied separately, are each small, mechanical, and easy to verify in isolation (one line added to an except tuple, one block widened to include the per-attempt body) with a dedicated regression test and mutation-test per site -- lower risk than a simultaneous refactor-plus-fix, even at the cost of real duplication. The round-2 review's own phrasing ('either is acceptable') and the fact that the extraction is already a tracked, scoped checklist item on the followups-followups task (which explicitly proposes the `_commit_with_version_retry(db, position_id, attempt_fn, max_attempts, on_row_gone)` shape and explicitly calls out that it 'would also be the natural single place to fix this same review's blocking finding... once instead of twice') both support deferring the extraction to that task's own dedicated pass, where it can get its own focused review rather than riding along on this one's already-long review history. The duplication cost of not extracting now is bounded and already fully tracked on the board, not silently accepted.

comments.summary: Round 2's two blocking findings (unhandled `ObjectDeletedError` escaping both `_merge_and_commit`'s and `_delete_position_and_commit`'s re-query-failure paths when the row is genuinely deleted by a different concurrent transaction in that exact window) are correctly fixed. Independently verified rather than taken on trust: confirmed via `issubclass()` against the actually-installed `sqlalchemy==2.1.0` that `ObjectDeletedError` is not a subclass of any of `StaleDataError`/`IntegrityError`/`OperationalError`; read the current (not diffed) code at backend/app/api/routers/portfolio.py:1043-1063 and confirmed the `ClosedTradeORM` construction and `db.delete(row)` are now genuinely inside the `try` block, not just the except clause having changed; mutation-tested both fixes myself by reverting each except tuple to the 3-type form and confirming both new regression tests then fail with the exact raw, unhandled `ObjectDeletedError` traceback described by the finding, then restored and reconfirmed the full suite green with zero residual diff.

Verified the two new regression tests' 'genuine, not mocked' `ObjectDeletedError` claim by reading both test bodies: each performs a real `delete()` + `commit()` of the row (via the saved original, unmocked bound methods) inside the mocked re-query function before raising the simulated `OperationalError`, so the row is actually gone in the DB when the next loop iteration's attribute access triggers SQLAlchemy's real expired-instance refresh path -- not a directly-raised fabrication. Cross-checked empirically with a standalone script: `Session.get()` on an expired, now-genuinely-deleted identity returns `None` cleanly rather than raising, confirming why the fix correctly needed to widen the per-attempt body's `try` (where the attribute-access-triggered refresh actually occurs) rather than relying on the re-query call itself to surface the exception.

Re-walked the full branching logic of both functions one more time for any other exception type that could slip through (per this round's explicit ask, given 2 prior rounds each found a genuine gap). No further gap found: the re-query calls themselves (a `Query.filter().one_or_none()` for merge, `Session.get()` for delete) cannot raise `ObjectDeletedError` -- confirmed empirically that behavior is specific to attribute-access-triggered refresh on an already-loaded, expired instance, not a fresh query/get -- so the inner `except OperationalError` scoped to just the re-query remains correct. `_merge_position`'s own `HTTPException(422)` (merge-overflow case) isn't one of the caught types and correctly propagates immediately rather than being retried. `watchlist.py` has no `version_id_col`/stale-row-attribute-read shape at all, so it's correctly out of scope for this bug class. Pool-exhaustion/connection-level errors aren't handled by either loop, but that's a pre-existing, unrelated failure class, not a `version_id_col`/re-query interaction -- out of scope for this review's mandate.

The decision not to extract a shared retry-loop helper as part of this fix (applying the identical narrow fix to each function separately instead) is reasonable, not corner-cutting: each fix is small (one except-tuple addition, one try-widening), independently mutation-tested, and the extraction itself is already a scoped, tracked checklist item on backend-position-watchlist-race-condition-followups-followups.json (item 4) rather than dropped.

Everything else verified clean this round: full backend suite 1613 passed, 100% line/branch coverage (gate 90%); ruff clean; mypy clean (correctly scoped via `[tool.mypy]`'s `files = ["app"]`); zero frontend diff in round 3 (confirmed via `git diff --stat`), and `yarn lint`/`yarn tsc -b --noEmit` both clean regardless; `python scripts/export_openapi.py` reproduces `backend/openapi.json` byte-for-byte (no API-contract-visible change, consistent with this being purely internal error-handling hardening); profit-target stale-wording guard clean. UI-facing check: `DELETE /api/portfolio/positions/{id}` has a frontend consumer, and since round 3 has zero API-visible/frontend diff, re-ran the persisted e2e suite (`make e2e`) rather than repeating round 2's already-passing manual walkthrough of unchanged behavior -- 27/27 specs passed, including the add-and-close-position golden path through the exact endpoint this round's fix touches. Elder/Analyse.md conformance: not applicable, confirmed via diff across all three rounds -- zero `app/signals/`/`app/portfolio/risk.py` changes.

review.notes: accepted (round 3). Round 2's two blocking findings (unhandled ObjectDeletedError in both _merge_and_commit's and _delete_position_and_commit's re-query-failure paths) are correctly and thoroughly fixed, verified via independent mutation testing, a from-scratch exhaustive branching re-trace, and confirmation that the regression tests' genuine-ObjectDeletedError claim holds up (real delete+commit inside the mock, not a fabricated raise). No new blocking findings. This PR had 2 genuine blocking bugs caught across rounds 1-2 of careful review; round 3's fix holds up under the same level of scrutiny. No new non-blocking findings beyond what's already tracked on backend-position-watchlist-race-condition-followups-followups.json.
